newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin to summon security aides to tackle crime.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin to summon security aides to tackle crime.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin, who has been concentrating on boosting economic and military reforms, plans to call in his top security officials to step up his fight against crime and corruption.

Itar-Tass news agency quoted Mikhail Mityukov, deputy secretary of Yeltsin's Security Council, as saying the Kremlin leader would summon the policy-making body "in the near future" to consider ways to fight crime.

"The crime situation has become a key destabilising factor which harms social and economic reforms and threatens national security," Mityukov said. He did not specify when Yeltsin planned to summon the council.
In the latest of many violent crimes, a banker who was also an aide to a nationalist member of parliament was shot dead in his car on Monday.

Police said the banker, Stanislav Alymov, was shot at point-bank range with a bazooka and finished off in cold blood with shots from Kalashnikov assault rifles. The police did not comment on the possible motive for the attack.
Mityukov said the government's failure to curb crime and corruption were feeding public distrust and scepticism about its ability to handle other major problems.
The poor state of the economy and unemployment have also contributed to a considerable increase in street crime.

Interfax news agency quoted Deputy Prosecutor General Yuri Chaika as saying the crime rate had grown by 50 percent and the number of homicides has doubled in the last few years. He gave no exact dates.
Russia was left with a poorly functioning judicial system after the Soviet Union and communist rule in 1991.

Financial hardships have led to a major decline of the law-enforcement agencies. Criminal gangs and underworld mafia-type cartels have taken control of a large part of Russia's economy and established links with corrupt officials.
Interfax quoted Deputy Interior Minister Pavel Maslyukov as saying the police were aware of more than 9,000 major criminal groups controlling 40,000 enterprises, including 499 banks.

"The corruption situation is very bad," Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov said in an interview published on Tuesday by the government daily newspaper Rossiyskaya Gazeta. "It has deeply penetrated the power structures."
Kulikov said police had recently seized a criminal group in Siberia and discovered a detailed plan for it to take control of almost all the local authorities.
"It was full of details about what should be done to take control of a certain official by a certain time," Kulikov said.

Yeltsin put fighting crime and corruption high on his list of promises in his re-election campaign last year but health problems limited the 66-year-old leader's scope to act in the first eight months of his new term.

But he told civil servants and state officials earlier this year to present statements on their incomes and spending every year. Several high-ranking officials, including top generals, have been charged with corruption. Mityukov said the full extent of crime in Russia remained unclear. "Everyone knows there is organised crime and corruption closely linked to it, but so far no one has full and true information about how big it really is," he said.
